source: NCERT Class VIII, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, History Ch. 1.

sections.heading: 1. The Decline of the Mughals
points: After **Aurangzeb's death (1707)**, weak successors, court factions and financial strain weakened the Mughal Empire.
**Nadir Shah** of Persia **sacked Delhi (1739)**, taking the **Peacock Throne** and the **Kohinoor**.
**Ahmad Shah Abdali** invaded repeatedly and defeated the Marathas at the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)**.
Mughal authority shrank to areas near Delhi.

sections.heading: 2. Rise of Regional Powers
points: These powers fought each other, leaving no single authority — a fragmented political map.

sections.heading: 3. The Coming of the Europeans
points: European trading companies — **Portuguese, Dutch, English and French** — competed for Indian trade.
The **English East India Company** exploited India's political fragmentation, winning **Plassey (1757)** and **Buxar (1764)**.
The **grant of the Diwani (1765)** gave it revenue control of Bengal → the beginning of British territorial rule.

sections.heading: 4. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Aurangzeb died 1707 → Mughal decline; Nadir Shah sacked Delhi 1739 (Peacock Throne, Kohinoor).
Third Battle of Panipat 1761 = Abdali defeated the Marathas.
Successor states: Hyderabad, Awadh, Bengal; new states: Marathas, Sikhs, Jats.
Political fragmentation opened the way for British expansion.

sections.heading: 5. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: **Nadir Shah (1739)** and **Ahmad Shah Abdali (Panipat 1761)** are different invaders.
**Successor states** stayed nominally loyal to the Mughals; **new states** rose in opposition.
**Diwani (1765)** gave the Company **revenue** power over Bengal-Bihar-Orissa.
The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) weakened the **Marathas**, not the British.
